opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they're complementary, but they're doing pretty different things. Pre-training is incredibly information-dense in one sense: you're getting a gradient signal on every single token, so the model soaks up a huge amount about the world, how language works, how people reason, how code is structured. It's building this enormous prior. But it's learning to imitate the distribution of what's out there, not necessarily to *achieve* anything.

RL flips that. The signal is much sparser. You might do a long trajectory of work and get a single bit at the end: did the tests pass, was the proof correct. So per sample you're learning far less. But what you're learning is much more targeted. You're directly reinforcing the behaviors that lead to success, and the model can discover strategies that weren't well represented in the pre-training data, like noticing it made a mistake, backtracking, or trying a different approach.

The interesting thing over the last year or two is that we've crossed a threshold where RL on these models actually works for real tasks. For a long time people were skeptical, because RL is famously finicky. But once you have a strong enough pre-trained base, the model already does the right thing some meaningful fraction of the time, and RL can amplify that. If the base model never succeeds, you get no signal and nothing to reinforce.

So my mental model is that pre-training gives you the raw material and the breadth, and RL teaches the model to deploy that knowledge reliably toward a goal. A big open question is how far RL can push into genuinely new capabilities versus mostly eliciting things that were latent. I think the evidence increasingly suggests it can teach real new skills, especially over longer horizons, as long as you have good, verifiable reward signals. Building those environments and feedback loops is now one of the main bottlenecks, maybe more than compute.

r001.rationale: It contrasts token-level gradient signals with sparse RL feedback, but does not say that discrete actions prevent gradients from being computed through the actions.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training as providing a gradient signal on every token and RL as much sparser, with less learning per sample, presenting pre-training as more learning-efficient.

r003.rationale: It calls pre-training and RL complementary and does not propose replacing next-token prediction or doing all model learning through RL.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that they're doing fundamentally different jobs, and the interesting question is less "which one is better" and more "what does each one actually buy you per unit of compute."

Pre-training is this incredibly dense signal. Every token is a supervision event. You're getting a gradient from basically every position in the sequence, and you're learning the entire structure of human knowledge as a side effect of trying to predict the next thing. It's almost embarrassingly efficient in that sense. The problem is that the ceiling is set by what's in the data. You're learning to imitate, and imitation only gets you to roughly the distribution of what people have already written down.

RL is the opposite profile. The signal is incredibly sparse. You might do a thousand tokens of reasoning and get one bit back at the end, did you get the right answer or not. So in terms of information per token, it's terrible. But the thing it gives you that pre-training can't is the ability to go beyond the data. You're not matching a distribution, you're optimizing against an outcome. And that means the model can discover strategies, ways of decomposing a problem, ways of checking its own work, that nobody wrote down, because nobody had to.

And I think the thing that surprised a lot of people over the last couple of years is how much of the capability gain was unlocked by RL once you had a strong enough base. Those two things interact. RL on a weak base doesn't do much, because the model can't stumble onto the right behavior often enough to get any signal. But once pre-training has given you a model that gets the right answer, say, one time in a hundred, now RL has something to grab onto, and it can take that from one percent to ninety percent remarkably quickly. So pre-training is building the search space, and RL is doing the search.

The other thing I'd say is that RL is really a story about where you can get verifiable reward. Math and code took off first precisely because you can check the answer. The frontier now is pushing that into domains where the reward is softer, where you need learned judges or environments that are more like the real world, and that's where a lot of the hard engineering actually is. It's less about the algorithm and much more about constructing environments and signals that don't get gamed.

So if you forced me to compress it: pre-training is how the model learns what the world is like, and RL is how it learns to actually do things in it. And right now, the marginal unit of compute going into RL is probably buying more capability than the marginal unit going into pre-training, but only because we spent years getting the pre-training foundation good enough for that to be true.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts dense token-level pre-training signals with sparse RL rewards, but does not discuss discrete actions or gradients through them.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training as an “incredibly dense signal” with supervision at every token and says RL provides very little information per token, presenting pre-training as more learning-efficient.

r003.rationale: The response treats pre-training and RL as doing different jobs and does not state that an RL formulation could replace next-token prediction or perform all learning through RL.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that pre-training lets you learn from an enormous amount of other people’s experience, whereas reinforcement learning lets you learn from the consequences of your own actions. Those are complementary. You wouldn’t want to discover everything by trial and error, but you also wouldn’t expect reading about a task to be the best possible way to master it.

There’s a question about whether RL is teaching models new abilities or just eliciting abilities they already have. Suppose a model can solve a problem once in a thousand attempts, and after RL it solves it reliably. You could call that elicitation, but making a useful behavior reliable is a substantial part of learning. The more interesting test is whether that process eventually lets the model solve problems it couldn’t practically solve before, by building on those intermediate skills.

The bottleneck is getting good feedback. With pre-training, you have a very broad source of supervision: predict the next token across all these different kinds of text. With RL, you need environments where success is measurable and where improving at the reward actually means improving at the task. That’s much easier for something like code, where you can run a test, than for a long research project where you might not know for months whether you made a good decision.

So I’d think of pre-training as giving you a broad starting point, and RL as a way to turn that starting point into increasingly competent behavior through practice. How far that goes depends a lot on the quality and diversity of the practice we can provide.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss discrete actions or difficulty computing gradients through them.

r002.rationale: It contrasts broad pre-training supervision with RL feedback bottlenecks, but does not clearly say pre-training is more learning-efficient.

r003.rationale: It does not propose replacing next-token prediction with an RL formulation or performing all learning through RL.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting distinction is between learning from what other people have done and learning from trying things yourself. In pre-training, you’re absorbing this enormous collection of human experience. With reinforcement learning, you can attempt a problem, see whether your approach worked, and adjust. That gives you a way to improve in places where there aren’t already good demonstrations to imitate.

But I wouldn’t draw a sharp line where pre-training gives you knowledge and reinforcement learning gives you reasoning. Pre-training clearly teaches a lot of reasoning, and reinforcement learning can teach you things about the world. The question is how much useful learning you can get out of each additional unit of compute.

The exciting possibility is that you get a loop: the model becomes capable enough to tackle harder problems, those problems provide useful feedback, and that feedback makes it more capable still. The difficulty is making sure the feedback actually rewards the ability you care about. For code, you can run tests. For a mathematical problem, you might be able to verify the answer. For a long research project, it’s much harder to tell whether a particular step was productive.

So I see them as complementary. Pre-training gives you an extraordinarily strong starting point. Reinforcement learning gives you a route to learning through experience, potentially beyond what’s represented in the training data. How far that route takes us depends a lot on the environments and feedback we can provide.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning from demonstrations with learning from experience, but does not mention discrete actions or difficulty computing gradients through them.

r002.rationale: It asks how much useful learning comes from each unit of compute, but does not present pre-training as presumably more learning-efficient than reinforcement learning.

r003.rationale: It describes pre-training and reinforcement learning as complementary; it does not say an RL formulation could replace next-token prediction or perform all learning through RL.
